title: Networking & latency math
description: Latency and network reps for the deep-dive half of a system-design interview: count the handshake round trips (RTTs) before the first byte, size the bandwidth-delay product and watch a small TCP window cap throughput, read p50/p99 by nearest rank, see tail latency compound across a fan-out, fit retries inside a deadline, cascade timeout budgets down a call chain, time a payload on the wire, and spend a latency SLO as a request budget. The conversions are named (1 Mbps = 125,000 bytes/s = 125 bytes/ms, 86,400 s/day) and probabilities are per-mille or parts-per-million, so every answer is an exact integer.

exercises.title: Round trips before the first byte
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A browser opens a fresh HTTPS connection to your API. The network round trip is 80 ms and the TLS handshake needs 2 round trips. How long until the first byte of the response arrives?"

**Why it works.** Before any data flows, a new connection pays fixed round trips: **1 RTT** for the TCP handshake, then the TLS handshake (**2 RTTs** for TLS 1.2, **1 RTT** for TLS 1.3, **0** for a resumed 0-RTT session), then **1 RTT** for the request/response itself. Time to first byte on a cold connection is therefore `(2 + tlsRtts) × rtt` — which is why keep-alive and TLS 1.3 matter more than most code changes.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `requestRtts(tlsRtts)` → `2 + tlsRtts` (TCP + TLS + the request itself)
- `timeToFirstByteMs(rttMs, tlsRtts)` → `requestRtts(tlsRtts) × rttMs`

**Worked example.** rtt 80 ms, TLS 1.2 (2 RTTs) → 4 round trips → **320 ms** before the first byte.

tests.name: TLS 1.3 (1 RTT) -> 3 round trips
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.requestRtts, 'function', 'export a function named requestRtts');
assert.equal(mod.requestRtts(1), 3);

tests.name: TLS 1.2 (2 RTTs) -> 4 round trips
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.requestRtts, 'function', 'export a function named requestRtts');
assert.equal(mod.requestRtts(2), 4);

tests.name: resumed 0-RTT session -> 2 round trips (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.requestRtts, 'function', 'export a function named requestRtts');
assert.equal(mod.requestRtts(0), 2);

tests.name: 100 ms RTT, TLS 1.3 -> 300 ms to first byte
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.timeToFirstByteMs, 'function', 'export a function named timeToFirstByteMs');
assert.equal(mod.timeToFirstByteMs(100, 1), 300);

tests.name: 80 ms RTT, TLS 1.2 -> 320 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.timeToFirstByteMs, 'function', 'export a function named timeToFirstByteMs');
assert.equal(mod.timeToFirstByteMs(80, 2), 320);

tests.name: 15 ms same-region RTT, TLS 1.3 -> 45 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.timeToFirstByteMs, 'function', 'export a function named timeToFirstByteMs');
assert.equal(mod.timeToFirstByteMs(15, 1), 45);

exercises.explanation:
Count the fixed round trips first, then multiply by the network RTT.

For `timeToFirstByteMs(80, 2)`:
- round trips = 1 (TCP) + 2 (TLS 1.2) + 1 (request) = 4
- TTFB = 4 × 80 = **320 ms**

The payload has not even started: this is pure handshake tax. Connection reuse (keep-alive) pays it once instead of per request, and TLS 1.3 cuts one RTT from every cold connection.
hints: A cold connection pays round trips before any response data: TCP first, then TLS, then the request itself.
Round trips = 1 (TCP) + tlsRtts (TLS) + 1 (request/response). Multiply the total by the network RTT for the time.
Add 2 to tlsRtts for the trip count, and time to first byte is that count × rttMs. No loops, no conditionals — two one-line functions.

exercises.title: Bandwidth-delay product and the window cap
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our two data centres are joined by a 100 Mbps link with a 40 ms round trip. How many bytes must be in flight to keep the link full — and why does a bulk copy with a 64 KiB TCP window crawl no matter how much bandwidth we buy?"

**Why it works.** The **bandwidth-delay product** (BDP) is how much data fits "in the pipe" during one round trip: rate × RTT. 1 Mbps = 1,000,000 bits/s = **125,000 bytes/s = 125 bytes/ms**, so the bytes in flight are `mbps × 125 × rttMs` (the 125,000 bytes/s and the ÷ 1,000 for milliseconds collapse to × 125). A TCP sender may have at most one **window** of unacknowledged bytes outstanding before it must wait for ACKs, so it delivers at most one window per round trip: `windowBytes × 1000 / rttMs` bytes per second (1,000 ms in a second). When the window is smaller than the BDP, the window — not the bandwidth — sets the throughput.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `bdpBytes(mbps, rttMs)` → `mbps × 125 × rttMs`
- `windowLimitedBytesPerSec(windowBytes, rttMs)` → `windowBytes × 1000 / rttMs`

The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Worked example.** 100 Mbps with a 40 ms RTT → 100 × 125 × 40 = **500,000 bytes** must be in flight to keep the link full.

tests.name: 100 Mbps x 40 ms -> 500,000 bytes in flight
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.bdpBytes, 'function', 'export a function named bdpBytes');
assert.equal(mod.bdpBytes(100, 40), 500000);

tests.name: 1 Gbps x 16 ms -> 2,000,000 bytes in flight
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.bdpBytes, 'function', 'export a function named bdpBytes');
assert.equal(mod.bdpBytes(1000, 16), 2000000);

tests.name: 50 Mbps x 8 ms -> 50,000 bytes in flight
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.bdpBytes, 'function', 'export a function named bdpBytes');
assert.equal(mod.bdpBytes(50, 8), 50000);

tests.name: 64 KiB window, 32 ms RTT -> 2,048,000 bytes/s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.windowLimitedBytesPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named windowLimitedBytesPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.windowLimitedBytesPerSec(65536, 32), 2048000);

tests.name: 125,000-byte window, 100 ms RTT -> 1,250,000 bytes/s
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.windowLimitedBytesPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named windowLimitedBytesPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.windowLimitedBytesPerSec(125000, 100), 1250000);

tests.name: window = BDP fills the 100 Mbps pipe exactly (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.windowLimitedBytesPerSec, 'function', 'export a function named windowLimitedBytesPerSec');
assert.equal(mod.windowLimitedBytesPerSec(500000, 40), 12500000);

exercises.explanation:
The sender can push only one window per round trip, then it waits for ACKs.

For `windowLimitedBytesPerSec(65536, 32)`:
- one window = 65,536 bytes, delivered once every 32 ms
- per second: 65,536 × 1000 = 65,536,000; ÷ 32 = **2,048,000 bytes/s** (about 16 Mbps)

That ceiling holds no matter how fat the pipe is: on long, fast links you raise the window (TCP window scaling) up to the BDP instead of buying bandwidth.
hints: Bytes in flight = sending rate × the time until the first ACK comes back. A sender can have only one window unacknowledged per round trip.
BDP = mbps × 125 bytes/ms × rttMs. Window-limited rate = windowBytes × 1000 ÷ rttMs bytes/s.
BDP multiplies mbps × 125 × rttMs, while the window-limited rate is windowBytes × 1000 ÷ rttMs — one full window per round trip.

exercises.title: p50 and p99 by nearest rank
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Here are ten response times from a load test, already sorted: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 25, 30, 80, 200 ms. What are p50 and p90 — and why do we alert on the tail, not the average?"

**Why it works.** With the **nearest-rank** method, the p-th percentile of `count` sorted samples is the sample at rank ⌈count × p / 100⌉, counting ranks from 1. There is no interpolation: the answer is always a latency somebody actually saw. Arrays are zero-based, so the index is that rank minus 1.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `percentileIndex(count, p)` → `Math.ceil(count × p / 100) − 1` (the zero-based nearest-rank index; `p` is 1..100)
- `percentileOf(sortedMs, p)` → `sortedMs[percentileIndex(sortedMs.length, p)]` (`sortedMs` is non-empty and sorted ascending)

**Worked example.** 100 samples, p99 → ⌈100 × 99 / 100⌉ = 99th smallest → zero-based index **98**.

tests.name: p50 of 100 samples -> index 49
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.percentileIndex, 'function', 'export a function named percentileIndex');
assert.equal(mod.percentileIndex(100, 50), 49);

tests.name: p99 of 100 samples -> index 98
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.percentileIndex, 'function', 'export a function named percentileIndex');
assert.equal(mod.percentileIndex(100, 99), 98);

tests.name: p95 of 10 samples -> index 9, the max (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.percentileIndex, 'function', 'export a function named percentileIndex');
assert.equal(mod.percentileIndex(10, 95), 9);

tests.name: p50 of the load-test sample -> 18 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.percentileOf, 'function', 'export a function named percentileOf');
assert.equal(mod.percentileOf([10,12,14,16,18,20,25,30,80,200], 50), 18);

tests.name: p90 of the load-test sample -> 80 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.percentileOf, 'function', 'export a function named percentileOf');
assert.equal(mod.percentileOf([10,12,14,16,18,20,25,30,80,200], 90), 80);

tests.name: p100 of the load-test sample -> 200 ms, the max (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.percentileOf, 'function', 'export a function named percentileOf');
assert.equal(mod.percentileOf([10,12,14,16,18,20,25,30,80,200], 100), 200);

exercises.explanation:
Find the rank, shift it to zero-based, then read the sorted sample.

For `percentileOf([10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 25, 30, 80, 200], 90)`:
- rank = ⌈10 × 90 / 100⌉ = ⌈9⌉ = 9
- index = 9 − 1 = 8
- sortedMs[8] = **80 ms**

The same sample has p50 = 18 ms, p90 = 80 ms and max = 200 ms: an average blends those into one number that describes nobody, which is why SLOs and alerts are written on percentiles.
hints: Nearest rank picks a real sample: the smallest value with at least p% of the samples at or below it.
rank = ⌈count × p ÷ 100⌉ (counting from 1), index = rank − 1, answer = the sorted sample at that index.
Rank = ceiling of count × p ÷ 100, minus 1 because arrays are zero-based — then index the sorted sample.

exercises.title: Tail latency at fan-out
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Each backend answers within 100 ms 99% of the time. A page calls 3 of them in parallel and waits for all of them. What fraction of page loads is slow?"

**Why it works.** The page is fast only when **every** call is fast, and independent "and" events multiply. We keep it integer: the per-backend chance of being fast is in **per-mille** (990‰ = 99%) and the result is in **parts per million** (ppm: 1,000,000 = 100%). Start at 1,000,000 ppm and, once per backend, multiply by `fastPermille` and divide by 1,000. The share of pages that hit at least one slow call is whatever is left of the million.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `allFastPpm(fastPermille, fanout)` → start from `1,000,000`; repeat `fanout` times: `ppm × fastPermille / 1000`
- `anySlowPpm(fastPermille, fanout)` → `1,000,000 − allFastPpm(fastPermille, fanout)`

The tests choose inputs (per-mille values that are multiples of 10, fan-out at most 5) for which every step stays whole — multiply before you divide.

**Worked example.** 950‰ fast, fan-out 2 → 1,000,000 × 950 / 1000 = 950,000 → × 950 / 1000 = **902,500 ppm** all-fast.

tests.name: 990 per-mille fast, fan-out 2 -> 980,100 ppm
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.allFastPpm, 'function', 'export a function named allFastPpm');
assert.equal(mod.allFastPpm(990, 2), 980100);

tests.name: 990 per-mille fast, fan-out 3 -> 970,299 ppm
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.allFastPpm, 'function', 'export a function named allFastPpm');
assert.equal(mod.allFastPpm(990, 3), 970299);

tests.name: 950 per-mille fast, fan-out 2 -> 902,500 ppm
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.allFastPpm, 'function', 'export a function named allFastPpm');
assert.equal(mod.allFastPpm(950, 2), 902500);

tests.name: 900 per-mille fast, fan-out 4 -> 656,100 ppm
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.allFastPpm, 'function', 'export a function named allFastPpm');
assert.equal(mod.allFastPpm(900, 4), 656100);

tests.name: 1000 per-mille fast, fan-out 5 -> 1,000,000 ppm, nothing is ever slow (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.allFastPpm, 'function', 'export a function named allFastPpm');
assert.equal(mod.allFastPpm(1000, 5), 1000000);

tests.name: fan-out 1 is the backend itself -> 10,000 ppm slow (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.anySlowPpm, 'function', 'export a function named anySlowPpm');
assert.equal(mod.anySlowPpm(990, 1), 10000);

tests.name: 990 per-mille fast, fan-out 3 -> 29,701 ppm slow
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.anySlowPpm, 'function', 'export a function named anySlowPpm');
assert.equal(mod.anySlowPpm(990, 3), 29701);

tests.name: 900 per-mille fast, fan-out 2 -> 190,000 ppm slow
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.anySlowPpm, 'function', 'export a function named anySlowPpm');
assert.equal(mod.anySlowPpm(900, 2), 190000);

exercises.explanation:
Multiply the per-backend fast chance once per hop, then take the rest of the million.

For `anySlowPpm(990, 3)`:
- start 1,000,000
- × 990 / 1000 = 990,000
- × 990 / 1000 = 980,100
- × 990 / 1000 = 970,299 ppm all-fast
- slow = 1,000,000 − 970,299 = **29,701 ppm** (about 3%)

This is the same multiplication as 03/02 availability-ppm (availabilities in series), read as tail latency: a per-backend p99 becomes roughly a page-level p97 at fan-out 3, and it keeps sliding as the fan-out grows.
hints: The page is fast only if every parallel call is fast — independent "and" events multiply.
allFast = 1,000,000 × (fastPermille ÷ 1000) applied fanout times. anySlow = 1,000,000 − allFast.
Start from 1,000,000 ppm and multiply by fastPermille ÷ 1000 once per backend — the slow share is one million minus that.

exercises.title: How many tries fit in the deadline
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our caller gives us a 1-second deadline. Each attempt to the payment service times out at 300 ms and we wait 100 ms before trying again. How many full attempts fit before the caller gives up?"

**Why it works.** In the worst case every try burns its whole timeout `T`, and there is a backoff `B` **between** tries but none after the last. So `t` tries cost `t × T + (t − 1) × B`. That must fit in the deadline `D`: `t × T + (t − 1) × B ≤ D` rearranges to `t × (T + B) ≤ D + B`, so `t` is `(D + B) / (T + B)` rounded **down**. A try that cannot finish inside the deadline is wasted work — the caller has already gone.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `triesWithinDeadline(deadlineMs, tryTimeoutMs, backoffMs)` → `Math.floor((deadlineMs + backoffMs) / (tryTimeoutMs + backoffMs))`
- `timeUsedMs(tryTimeoutMs, backoffMs, tries)` → `tries × tryTimeoutMs + (tries − 1) × backoffMs` (defined for `tries ≥ 1`)

**Worked example.** 1,000 ms deadline, 300 ms timeout, 100 ms backoff → (1,000 + 100) / (300 + 100) = 1,100 / 400, rounded down = **2 tries**; they use 2 × 300 + 1 × 100 = 700 ms.

tests.name: 1,000 ms deadline, 300 ms tries, 100 ms backoff -> 2 tries
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.triesWithinDeadline, 'function', 'export a function named triesWithinDeadline');
assert.equal(mod.triesWithinDeadline(1000, 300, 100), 2);

tests.name: 2,000 ms deadline, 400 ms tries, 100 ms backoff -> 4 tries
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.triesWithinDeadline, 'function', 'export a function named triesWithinDeadline');
assert.equal(mod.triesWithinDeadline(2000, 400, 100), 4);

tests.name: no backoff: 900 ms deadline, 300 ms tries -> 3 tries (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.triesWithinDeadline, 'function', 'export a function named triesWithinDeadline');
assert.equal(mod.triesWithinDeadline(900, 300, 0), 3);

tests.name: deadline shorter than one try -> 0 tries (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.triesWithinDeadline, 'function', 'export a function named triesWithinDeadline');
assert.equal(mod.triesWithinDeadline(250, 300, 50), 0);

tests.name: 2 tries of 300 ms with 100 ms backoff -> 700 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.timeUsedMs, 'function', 'export a function named timeUsedMs');
assert.equal(mod.timeUsedMs(300, 100, 2), 700);

tests.name: 4 tries of 400 ms with 100 ms backoff -> 1,900 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.timeUsedMs, 'function', 'export a function named timeUsedMs');
assert.equal(mod.timeUsedMs(400, 100, 4), 1900);

exercises.explanation:
Add one backoff to the deadline, divide by the cost of a try plus its backoff, round down.

For `triesWithinDeadline(2000, 400, 100)`:
- (2,000 + 100) / (400 + 100) = 2,100 / 500 = 4.2
- rounded down = **4 tries**
- check: 4 × 400 + 3 × 100 = 1,900 ms fits; a fifth try would end at 5 × 400 + 4 × 100 = 2,400 ms

03/06 retry-budget computes the worst-case total time a retry policy can burn; this drill is its inverse — given the caller's time, how many tries the policy may have before retries outlive the request.
hints: Every try can burn its full timeout, and the backoff sits between tries — there is none after the last one.
t × T + (t − 1) × B ≤ D, which rearranges to t ≤ (D + B) ÷ (T + B). Round down. Time used = t × T + (t − 1) × B.
t tries cost t × timeout + (t − 1) × backoff — add one backoff to the deadline and divide by (timeout + backoff), rounding down.

exercises.title: Timeout budgets down a call chain
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The edge gives each request 2 seconds. It calls service A, which calls B, which calls C, and every hop spends about 150 ms of its own overhead. What timeout should a service 4 hops deep use — and how deep can the chain go before the innermost hop has less than 500 ms to do real work?"

**Why it works.** Timeouts must **shrink** inward: each hop has to give up before its caller does, or its retries keep working for a caller that has already timed out. With a fixed per-hop overhead, the budget at depth `d` (depth 0 is the edge itself) is the edge timeout minus `d` overheads. The deepest useful hop is the largest `d` whose budget is still at least `minUsefulMs`: `edge − d × overhead ≥ minUseful` gives `d ≤ (edge − minUseful) / overhead`, rounded **down**.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `budgetAtDepth(edgeTimeoutMs, perHopOverheadMs, depth)` → `edgeTimeoutMs − depth × perHopOverheadMs`
- `maxDepth(edgeTimeoutMs, perHopOverheadMs, minUsefulMs)` → `Math.floor((edgeTimeoutMs − minUsefulMs) / perHopOverheadMs)`

**Worked example.** 2,000 ms at the edge, 150 ms per hop, 4 hops deep → 2,000 − 4 × 150 = **1,400 ms**.

tests.name: depth 0 is the edge itself -> 2,000 ms (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.budgetAtDepth, 'function', 'export a function named budgetAtDepth');
assert.equal(mod.budgetAtDepth(2000, 150, 0), 2000);

tests.name: 2,000 ms edge, 150 ms per hop, depth 4 -> 1,400 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.budgetAtDepth, 'function', 'export a function named budgetAtDepth');
assert.equal(mod.budgetAtDepth(2000, 150, 4), 1400);

tests.name: 1,000 ms edge, 250 ms per hop, depth 4 -> 0 ms, budget exhausted
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.budgetAtDepth, 'function', 'export a function named budgetAtDepth');
assert.equal(mod.budgetAtDepth(1000, 250, 4), 0);

tests.name: 2,000 ms edge, 150 ms per hop, 500 ms useful -> depth 10
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.maxDepth, 'function', 'export a function named maxDepth');
assert.equal(mod.maxDepth(2000, 150, 500), 10);

tests.name: 1,200 ms edge, 100 ms per hop, 450 ms useful -> depth 7
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.maxDepth, 'function', 'export a function named maxDepth');
assert.equal(mod.maxDepth(1200, 100, 450), 7);

exercises.explanation:
Spend the headroom above the useful minimum one overhead at a time.

For `maxDepth(2000, 150, 500)`:
- headroom = 2,000 − 500 = 1,500 ms
- 1,500 / 150 = 10, already whole, so **depth 10**
- check: budgetAtDepth(2000, 150, 10) = 2,000 − 1,500 = 500 ms, exactly the useful minimum

In production you propagate the remaining deadline with the request (a header or a gRPC deadline) instead of hard-coding per-service timeouts, so no inner hop works for a caller that is already gone.
hints: A hop deeper in the chain must give up before its caller does — each hop gets what it was handed minus its own overhead.
budget(d) = edge − d × overhead. The deepest d with budget(d) ≥ minUseful is ⌊(edge − minUseful) ÷ overhead⌋.
Each hop subtracts its overhead from what the caller handed down, so the deepest useful hop is (edge − minUseful) ÷ overhead, rounded down.

exercises.title: Payload time on the wire
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A JSON response is 1.25 MB and the client is on a 100 Mbps link. How long does the body take on the wire, and how long is the whole download with a 40 ms round trip?"

**Why it works.** Transfer (serialization) time is size divided by speed. 1 Mbps = 1,000,000 bits/s = 125,000 bytes/s = **125 bytes/ms**, so a link of `mbps` megabits moves `125 × mbps` bytes every millisecond. A simple download on an open connection pays one RTT for the request to go out and the first byte to come back, then the transfer. (01/04 sizes the aggregate egress of a whole fleet; this is the time for one response.)

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `transferMs(payloadBytes, mbps)` → `payloadBytes / (125 × mbps)`
- `downloadMs(payloadBytes, mbps, rttMs)` → `rttMs + transferMs(payloadBytes, mbps)`

The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Worked example.** 500,000 bytes on a 4 Mbps link → 500,000 / (125 × 4) = 500,000 / 500 = **1,000 ms**.

tests.name: 1,250,000 bytes on 100 Mbps -> 100 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.transferMs, 'function', 'export a function named transferMs');
assert.equal(mod.transferMs(1250000, 100), 100);

tests.name: 500,000 bytes on 4 Mbps -> 1,000 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.transferMs, 'function', 'export a function named transferMs');
assert.equal(mod.transferMs(500000, 4), 1000);

tests.name: empty body -> 0 ms (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.transferMs, 'function', 'export a function named transferMs');
assert.equal(mod.transferMs(0, 100), 0);

tests.name: 1,250,000 bytes on 100 Mbps after a 40 ms RTT -> 140 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.downloadMs, 'function', 'export a function named downloadMs');
assert.equal(mod.downloadMs(1250000, 100, 40), 140);

tests.name: 250,000 bytes on 20 Mbps after a 60 ms RTT -> 160 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.downloadMs, 'function', 'export a function named downloadMs');
assert.equal(mod.downloadMs(250000, 20, 60), 160);

exercises.explanation:
Convert the link to bytes per millisecond, divide, then add the round trip.

For `downloadMs(1250000, 100, 40)`:
- rate = 125 × 100 = 12,500 bytes/ms
- transfer = 1,250,000 / 12,500 = 100 ms
- download = 40 + 100 = **140 ms**

On slow mobile links the body dominates, so shrinking the payload (compression, pagination, fewer fields) often beats shaving server time.
hints: Time on the wire is size divided by speed — convert Mbps to bytes per millisecond first.
transfer = payloadBytes ÷ (125 × mbps) ms. download = rttMs + transfer.
One Mbps moves 125 bytes each millisecond, so the wire time is payloadBytes ÷ (125 × mbps) — a simple download adds one RTT in front.

exercises.title: A latency SLO as a request budget
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our SLO says 99% of requests finish under 200 ms. We serve 86.4 million requests a day (1,000 QPS average over 86,400 s/day). How many slow requests can we afford today, and how much is left after 600,000 have already been slow?"

**Why it works.** A latency SLO is a **count you can spend**. Written in per-mille (990‰ = 99%), the SLO leaves `1000 − sloPermille` per-mille of the day's requests allowed to be slow. Subtract the slow requests already served to get what is left; a negative number means the budget is blown and risky deploys should stop. 03/03 error-budget expresses the same idea as downtime minutes; here the budget is a request count.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `allowedSlowPerDay(requestsPerDay, sloPermille)` → `requestsPerDay × (1000 − sloPermille) / 1000`
- `slowBudgetLeft(requestsPerDay, sloPermille, slowSoFar)` → `allowedSlowPerDay(requestsPerDay, sloPermille) − slowSoFar` (negative = over budget)

The tests choose inputs that divide exactly, so every answer is a whole number.

**Worked example.** 5,000,000 requests a day at a 999‰ SLO → 5,000,000 × (1000 − 999) / 1000 = **5,000** slow requests allowed.

tests.name: 86,400,000 requests at 990 per-mille -> 864,000 slow allowed
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.allowedSlowPerDay, 'function', 'export a function named allowedSlowPerDay');
assert.equal(mod.allowedSlowPerDay(86400000, 990), 864000);

tests.name: 5,000,000 requests at 999 per-mille -> 5,000 slow allowed
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.allowedSlowPerDay, 'function', 'export a function named allowedSlowPerDay');
assert.equal(mod.allowedSlowPerDay(5000000, 999), 5000);

tests.name: a 100% SLO allows nothing -> 0 (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.allowedSlowPerDay, 'function', 'export a function named allowedSlowPerDay');
assert.equal(mod.allowedSlowPerDay(100000, 1000), 0);

tests.name: 864,000 allowed, 600,000 spent -> 264,000 left
tests.code:

exercises.explanation:
Turn the SLO into an allowance, then subtract what is already spent.

For `slowBudgetLeft(86400000, 990, 600000)`:
- allowance = 86,400,000 × (1000 − 990) / 1000 = 86,400,000 × 10 / 1000 = 864,000
- left = 864,000 − 600,000 = **264,000** slow requests

Same budget idea as 03/03 error-budget, counted in requests instead of downtime minutes: when it reaches zero (the 999‰ case is already at −1,500), the team stops shipping risky changes until the window rolls over.
hints: A 99% target means 1% of requests are ALLOWED to be slow — that 1% is a budget you spend.
allowed = requestsPerDay × (1000 − sloPermille) ÷ 1000. left = allowed − slowSoFar.
The slow allowance is the per-mille gap between 1000 and the SLO, applied to the day's request count. Subtract what you already burned — below zero means frozen deploys.
